Synchronous improvement of methane production and digestate 
dewaterability in sludge anaerobic digestion by nanobubble 
Tianfeng Wang a,*, Jie Wang a, Jiazi Niu a, Peilin Guo a, Cheng Peng a, Rixing He a, Zhou Hui a, 
Wenqi Gao b, Qingfang Zhang a 
a College of Petrochemical Engineering, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China 
b School of Civil Engineering, Lanzhou Institute of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Four different NBWs were added to the 
sludge anaerobic digestion. 
• The hydrolysis of sludge anaerobic 
digestion can be enhanced by the addi­
tion of NBW. 
• Addition of NBW increased methane 
production by 9.0–27.8% compared 
with control. 
• Addition of NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) 
improved 
the 
dewaterability 
of 
digestate. 
• Air-NBW was the most cost-effective 
additive for sludge anaerobic digestion.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Hydrolysis 
Ammonia nitrogen 
Sludge particle size 
Zeta potential 
Protein secondary structure 
A B S T R A C T   
The subsequence anaerobic digestion (AD) of dewatered sludge (DWS) from wastewater treatment plants ne­
cessitates an emphasis on enhancing methane production and dewaterability. The effect of different nanobubble 
water (NBW) on AD of DWS was investigated under mesophilic conditions. Cumulative methane production was 
improved by 9.0–27.8% with the addition of different NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2). NBW improved methanogenic 
performance by significantly enhancing the hydrolysis of sludge AD. Results from the digestate, the capillary 
suction time, specific resistance to filtration, and moisture content could be decreased by 14.6–18.2%, 
18.8–29.6%, and 13.6–19.5%, respectively. The addition of NBW can improve the dewaterability of digestate by 
reducing the digestate particle size and increasing the zeta potential of digestate. The addition of NBW signifi­
cantly increased methane production and improved dewaterability in AD; Air-NBW showed the best 
improvement.

1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is gaining widespread attention not only 
for its ability to convert dewatered sludge (DWS) into biogas but also for 
its ability to reduce environmental pollution significantly (Bala­
sundaram et al., 2023). However, it suffers from poor hydrolysis ca­
pacity, easy inhibition, long lag phase, and low biogas production 
(Mutegoa and Sahini, 2023). To facilitate subsequent processing, 
digestate usually undergoes dewatering using a belt filter press or a 
centrifugal dewatering machine (Simoni et al., 2024). Reducing the 
moisture content (MC: moisture content of DWS cake) of sludge is a key 
approach to reducing the cost of sludge management (Cao et al., 2023). 
Consequently, it is essential to discover appropriate techniques to 
enhance the AD performance and dewaterability of digestate in an 
economically feasible manner. 
The total solid (TS) of the sludge is an important factor during AD. 
Methane production showed an increasing and then decreasing trend 
when the TS increased, the optimal TS for AD under mesophilic condi­
tions should be around 8 % (An et al., 2017). However, the TS of DWS is 
usually up to about 20 % (Simoni et al., 2024). Therefore, the solids 
content of AD systems can be adjusted by adding other media to the 
digester. If this media can synchronously improve the sludge hydrolysis, 
methane yield, and digestate dewaterability, while ensuring the possi­
bility of land use of the digestate, it will have great application pros­
pects. Nanobubble water (NBW) is defined as water containing a large 
number of bubbles less than 1000 nm in diameter (Kurz et al., 2021), 
which has some distinct advantages, including robust adsorption ca­
pacity, increased gas solubility, extended retention time, and elevated 
zeta potential in comparison to deionized water (Zinjenab et al., 2023). 
NBW is non-polluting and its addition to the sludge AD system will not 
affect the subsequent treatment (Patel et al., 2021). 
N2-NBW increased cumulative methane production by 29.1 % of the 
sludge AD because the N2-NBW has a higher electrical charge, which can 
increase the zeta potential in the system by 17.1 % (Yang et al., 2019). 
An increase in zeta potential usually implies an increase in repulsive 
forces between sludge particles, which may result in the sludge flocs 
becoming more loosely packed, thus facilitating microbial-substrate 
contact and improving substrate availability, and thus increasing 
methane production (Marcelino et al., 2023). Air-NBW increased cu­
mulative methane production by 33.0 % of the sludge AD due to the 
enhanced microbial activity of Air-NBW, which enhances the activity of 
the electron transport system by 27.2 % (Hou et al., 2022). The benefits 
of NBW addition may include the promotion of substrate degradation 
(Fan et al., 2021b), avoiding acid inhibition (Fan et al., 2020), and 
mitigation of ammonia suppression (Fan et al., 2021b). The positive 
effects of NBW on methane production from sludge have been revealed 
in recent research, but its effect on digestate dewaterability is unclear. 
After traditional AD, the dewaterability of digestate severely dete­
riorated, thus improving the dewatering property of digestate has 
become one of the important tasks in this field (Cao et al., 2023; Simoni 
et al., 2024). After β-cyclodextrin pretreatment, the hydrolysis rate and 
cumulative methane production of AD increased by 153.2 % and 175.4 
%, respectively; meanwhile, the capillary suction time (CST) of digestate 
decreased by 24.1 % (Guo et al., 2022). The addition of biochar resulted 
in improved cumulative methane production (>23.1 %) and decreased 
digestate specific resistance of filtration (SRF) (>57.1 %) (Liang et al., 
2022). The addition of Ca(OH)2 increased cumulative methane pro­
duction by 33.3 %, improved digestate dewaterability, and decreased 
moisture content by 7.9 % due to an increase in digestate zeta potential 
(Li et al., 2017). The high surface charge and theoretically high Laplace 
pressure of nanobubble induce hydrophobic interaction (Marcelino 
et al., 2023), which applied to AD may enhance the dewaterability of 
digestate. The rise in methane generation appeared to be instrumental in 
enhancing the dewaterability of digestate; however, the impact of NBW 
addition on the dewaterability of digestate processed anaerobically has 
not been demonstrated. 
Therefore, this study selected four kinds of NBW prepared with 
cheap and safe gases (Air, CO2, He, and N2) to evaluate their effect on 
methane production of DWS, as well as the influence on the dewater­
ability of digestate. During the AD process, the methane production and 
the changes of soluble hydrolysate and acidification products were 
analyzed. The microbial community subjected to different NBWs was 
characterized and correlated to the profile of methane production. After 
digestion, the dewaterability of digestate was analyzed and the role of 
NBWs addition was discussed. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Materials 
DWS was acquired from a wastewater treatment plant in Lanzhou 
City, China, using the “oxidation ditch + aerated biofilter process” with 
a treatment scale of 5000 m3/d. DWS was cultivated under mesophilic 
conditions for 10 days to be used as inoculum. The table illustrates the 
properties of the inoculum and the substrate (see Supplementary 
Material). 
A nanobubble generator (JXWNP-AL01, Jinxiang, China) was uti­
lized to produce different types of NBW. The pressure of the nanobubble 
generator was maintained at 0.4–0.5 MPa. Air, CO2, He, and N2 were 
introduced into the machine separately to produce NBW using hydro­
dynamic cavitation. Then the gases were completely mixed with water 
and allowed to stationary for 10 min at 25 ± 2 ◦C to form the NBW. The 
reasons for choosing these four gases are as follows: Air: O2 can provide 
micro-oxygenic conditions for AD; CO2: CO2 can be involved in the 
synthesis of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis; He: He is an inert gas 
with relatively low molecular weight, and the effect on the AD of sludge 
is unclear; N2: N2 has inert characteristics with relatively high molecular 
weight (Kurz et al., 2021; Marcelino et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2019). 
The AD system was set up as described by Liu et al. (2022). Under 
mesophilic conditions, DWS was used as the substrate, seed sludge was 
used as inoculum; deionized water and different NBW were mixed 
proportionally (the mass mixing ratio was DWS: NBW: seed sludge =
682 g:682 g:136 g), and all of the reactants were loaded into the di­
gesters and gently stirred for 1 min to mix well. The digesters were 
prepared and put into a water bath (37 ± 2 ◦C) at the same time, the AD 
was carried out for a total of 35 days at mesophilic temperature. In this 
experiment, five experimental groups were set up with the addition of 
deionized water, Air-NBW, CO2-NBW, He-NBW, and N2-NBW. The five 
conditions were labeled as control, Air, CO2, He, and N2 groups, and 
three parallel experiments were conducted for each condition, with a 
total of 15 digesters. 
2.2. Methods of analysis 
On Day 4, 8, 15, 22, 28, and 35, an 80 g sample of the mixture was 
taken. The samples were centrifuged at 2000 g for 5 min, and the su­
pernatant was collected using a 0.45 µm polyethersulfone microfiber 
filter. The filtered liquid samples were used to determine the indicators. 
TS, volatile solid (VS), pH, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), 
and total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) were determined by standard 
methods (APAH,1998), and standard formulas in the literature calcu­
lated free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) (Hansen et al., 1998). Volatile fatty 
acid (VFA) and methane content were determined using a gas chro­
matograph (SP-7890Plus, Rui Hong, China), and the volume of biogas 
was determined using an acid gas flow meter (LML-2, Alpha, China). 
MC and SRF were measured as described by Zhang et al. (2024). CST 
was determined using a capillary water absorption meter (304 M, Triton 
Electronics, UK). The size of the digestate particles and their zeta po­
tential were analyzed using a nanoparticle size and zeta potential 
analyzer (Nano ZS90, Malvern, UK). The concentration of proteins and 
polysaccharides in EPS was assayed via a modified Lowry and Anthrone 
protocol (Chuenchart et al., 2021). Three-dimensional fluorescence

excitation and emission matrix (3D-EEM) scans were obtained using a 
fluorophotometer (F4600, Hitachi, Japan). 
DNA was extracted from digestate, and the microorganisms con­
tained therein were tested for abundance and type using high- 
throughput sequencing to determine differences in the microbial com­
munity in the digesters after adding different NBW. Primers 341F (5′- 
CCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGGTWTC­
TAAT-3′) were utilized to amplify the bacterial 16S rRNA gene in the V3- 
V4 portion of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene; using primers Arch519F (5′- 
CAGCCGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and Arch915R (5′-GTGCTCCCCCGCCAAT 
TCCT-3′) to amplify the V4 portion of the Archaea V4-V5 portion of the 
16S rRNA gene. Each sample was subjected to DNA extraction, followed 
by sequencing. Finally, initial data and detailed information on species 
were uploaded through the website (https://www. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). 
The accession numbers were PRJNA1066472 and PRJNA1066485. 
2.3. Statistical analysis 
The data were analyzed using SPSS (27.0), and the data from 
different experimental groups were analyzed for differences using 
ANOVA. The p < 0.05 indicates a significant difference between the two 
experimental groups. SPSS was also used to complete the principal 
component analysis (PCA) and Duncan’s test. Pearson correlation 
analysis was performed for microbial community, dewaterability, and 
environmental factors. Methane production was fitted to a modified 
Gompertz model (Balasundaram et al., 2023). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Anaerobic digestion performance 
VFA is an outcome of hydrolysis and acidification and a feedstock for 
biogas generation (Fan et al., 2021b). The maximum concentration of 
VFA was found from Day 4 to Day 8, which declined rapidly after Day 8, 
and stabilized after Day 22 (Fig. 1). On Day 4, the digesters with added 
NBW (Air, CO2, and He) significantly increased VFA by 17.9 % (p <
0.01), 20.7 % (p < 0.01), and 11.2 % (p < 0.05) compared with the 
control. The peak of VFA appeared earlier with the introduction of Air- 
NBW and CO2-NBW than with the addition of He-NBW and N2-NBW, 
likely as a result of the improved mass transfer performance of Air-NBW 
and CO2-NBW (He et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). The VFA of CO2-NBW 
group was at a high level for the longest period among the five groups. 
This phenomenon could be attributed to the introduction of CO2 nano­
bubbles which enhanced the activity of hydrolyzing bacteria, enhanced 
the degradation of organic matter, and participated in the process of 
methane production by the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (Chuen­
chart et al., 2021; Marcelino et al., 2023). 
The pH serves as a critical parameter in AD, with a range of 6.5 to 8.0 
being optimal for methanogens; an increase in pH will also lead to an 
increase in FAN (Goodarzi et al., 2024). All digesters showed similar pH 
trends, with the pH of the digesters ranging from 7.2 to 7.8 (Fig. 2a). As 
the AD proceeded, the pH value showed a decreasing and then 
increasing trend, and gradually stabilized, which was caused by the 
change of VFA in AD (Fan et al., 2021a). 
SCOD level indicates the hydrolysis and decomposition of sludge 
flocs (Liu et al., 2022). All digesters showed the same trend of SCOD

(Fig. 2b); all of them showed a trend of increasing first, peaking between 
Day 4 and Day 8, and then decreasing; the same trend as the VFA 
changes (Wang et al., 2024). On Day 8, the SCOD of four digesters added 
with NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) were significantly increased by 23.1 % 
(p < 0.01), 14.2 % (p < 0.01), 11.7 % (p < 0.01), and 12.8 % (p < 0.01), 
respectively, as compared with control. In terms of the maximum SCOD, 
the optimal hydrolysis-promoting effect was found in the digester with 
Air-NBW. Air-NBW created a micro-oxygenic environment in the early 
stage of AD, which promotes the growth of facultative anaerobes and 
electron transfer between microorganisms, leading to the promoted 
hydrolysis of the substrate (Hou et al., 2022). The promoting effect of 
He-NBW and N2-NBW showed less prominent, probably because the 
inert gases had less effect on the enzymes (Wang et al., 2023). 
Ammonia is a product of protein hydrolysis that increases gradually 
with AD (Liu et al., 2022). The trend of TAN changes in all digesters was 
consistent, with an increase followed by a gradual leveling off, which 
was maintained at 500–2000 mgN L-1 (Fig. 2c). It is worth noting that 
TAN higher than 1500 mgN L-1 may inhibit methanogens (Wang et al., 
2024). On Day 8, the TAN of digesters with added NBW (Air, CO2, He, 
and N2) were significantly increased by 22.8 % (p < 0.01), 12.1 % (p <
0.01), 24.7 % (p < 0.01), and 20.7 % (p < 0.01) as compared with the 
control. The addition of NBW can affect the activity of microorganisms 
because the properties of nanobubbles affect the growth and reproduc­
tion of microorganisms and their physiological activities (He et al., 
2022). On Day 35, the digesters with added NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) 
significantly increased TAN by 6.4 % (p < 0.01), 9.0 % (p < 0.01), 10.1 
% (p < 0.01), and 10.1 % (p < 0.01). The TAN difference (between 
added NBW and control) decreased from 160.3 to 181.3 mgN L-1 (Day 8) 
to 114.0–179.3 mgN L-1 (Day 35). This indicates that the addition of 
NBW can enhance sludge hydrolysis during the early stage of AD (Fan 
et al., 2021b). In addition, it has been reported that the addition of NBW 
can increase TAN in AD by 200–400 mgN L-1 on Day 4 and Day 10 (Fan 
et al., 2021a), which enhanced the hydrolysis in the early AD stage. 
FAN is a part of TAN, which is significant inhibitory to methanogens 
(Capson-Tojo et al., 2020). All digesters showed similar trends in FAN, 
with FAN ranging from 0 to 150 mgN L-1 (Fig. 2d). FAN would increase 
with the AD, and FAN would show a trend of increasing and becoming 
later. When the FAN > 250 mgN L-1, it would inhibit methanogens 
(Zhang et al., 2024). Consequently, the restraining influence of FAN on 
methanogens is confined. 
The digesters with added NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) significantly 
increased ultimate methane production by 27.9 % (p < 0.01), 32.0 % (p 
< 0.01), 16.0 % (p < 0.01), and 9.2 % (p < 0.05) compared with the 
control (Fig. 2e and Table 1). This is because nanobubbles can effec­
tively improve mass transfer, increase the activity of microbial com­
munity in the digesters, and expedite the breakdown of organic matter 
and the consumption of VFA (Hou et al., 2022). The highest cumulative 
methane production from CO2-NBW was confirmed by VFA and SCOD 
measurements, which demonstrated the beneficial effect of NBW addi­
tion in optimizing the AD process of the sludge (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2b). The 
lower cumulative methane production in the digesters of He and N2 may 
be a result of the higher TAN (Fig. 2c), as TAN above 1500 mgN L-1 
inhibits the activity of methanogens (Wang et al., 2024). As reported, 
the addition of Air-NBW and CO2-NBW increased cumulative methane 
production in the mesophilic digester by 20.8 % and 19.1 %, respec­
tively (Fan et al., 2020). Existing studies have concentrated on a weaker 
impact of NBW, this can be credited to the increased concentration of 
substrate organic material and the relatively lower volume of NBW 
employed per unit of VS in the latter. 
The methane production rate peaked on Day 7, NBW (Air, CO2, He, 
and N2) significantly increased the methane production rate by 44.8 % 
(p < 0.01), 37.9 % (p < 0.01), 20.4 % (p < 0.01), and 17.6 % (p < 0.05) 
compared with the control (Fig. 2e). Air-NBW enhanced the hydrolysis 
process in AD, and the organic matter available for microorganisms 
increased, leading to the highest methane production rate in Air-NBW 
on Day 7 (Fan et al., 2020). The cumulative methane production of 
He-NBW and N2-NBW was close, suggesting that these two nanobubbles 
mainly served to promote hydrolysis (Wang et al., 2023). Besides the 
promotion of hydrolysis, the micro-oxygenic environment created by air 
nanobubbles and the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis enhanced by 
CO2 nanobubbles may further improve the cumulative methane pro­
duction (Marcelino et al., 2023; Chuenchart et al., 2021). The Gompertz 
model verified that the addition of NBW could shorten the lag phase of 
the AD system (3.4–19.7 %); this may be because the nanobubbles had 
high stability and could exist in the digestion system for a long time. This 
stability helps to reduce the lag phase in the AD process (He et al., 2022). 
3.2. Microbial community 
A relationship exists between the types and roles of the anaerobic 
microbial population involved in biogas production (Bahadur et al., 
2024; Wu et al., 2021). It could be affected by the variety of feedstock, 
temperature, pH, TAN, and additional factors (Balasundaram et al., 
2023). Assessing microbial diversity aids in identifying the composition 
of the community that results in modifications of the methanogens (Wu 
et al., 2023). The microbial community was analyzed for operational 
taxonomic units (OTUs), Shannon, Chao1, and Simpson indexes (see 
Supplementary Material). The OTUs, Shannon and Chao1 indexes of 
bacteria showed that the AD system with the addition of Air-NBW had a 
higher number of species than in the control. This is because the intro­
duction of Air-NBW into the AD process increases the activity and di­
versity of the microbial community and promotes symbiotic interactions 
between different microbiota (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). 
Among the top ten archaea in relative abundance (RA), Methanosaeta 
and Methanospirillum are acetotrophic methanogens, while Meth­
anosarcina is a facultative methanogen, and the other seven species are 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Fig. 3a) (Akindolire et al., 2022; 
Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). On Day 8, the RA of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens in the NBW groups (62.5–90.1 %) was lower than that in 
the control (99.7 %); on Day 35, the RA of hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogens in the NBW groups (33.5–54.7 %) was higher than that in the 
control (21.6 %). Hydrogenotrophic methanogens mainly rely on H2 as 
an electron donor to reduce CO2 to methane during their metabolic 
processes (Akindolire et al., 2022). On Day 8, NBW promoted sludge 
hydrolysis, thus the SCOD in the NBW groups was higher than that of the 
control. On Day 35, the cumulative methane production in the NBW 
groups was higher than that of the control, resulting in a lower SCOD in 
the NBW groups than that of the control. The difference in dissolved 
organic matter may cause the difference in the RA of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens (Bahadur et al., 2024). 
A reduction in the RA of Methanobacterium, Methanobrevibacter, 
Methanocorpusculum, and Methanomassiliicoccus, which were hydro­

2018), were observed in the comparison between Day 8 and Day 35 
(Fig. 3a). Methanobacterium and Methanocorpusculum as methanogens 
have synergistic effects during AD and can engage with other metha­
nogens and fermenters to facilitate the degradation and transformation 
of organic substances (Ziganshina and Ziganshin, 2023). After correla­
tion analysis of archaea with anaerobic environmental factors, Meth­
anobacterium demonstrated a substantial positive correlation with SCOD 
(p < 0.01) (Fig. 3c). Methanocorpusculum exhibited a marked positive 
correlation alongside TAN (p < 0.01) and VFA (p < 0.01). This suggests 
that Methanobacterium and Methanocorpusculum are more adapted to the 
VFA environment. Methanobrevibacter presented a substantial positive 
correlation with acetic acid content and cumulative methane production 
(p < 0.05). Methanomassiliicoccus exhibited a notable negative correla­
tion in connection with TS (p < 0.05), and a substantial positive corre­
lation among cumulative methane production (p < 0.01). This suggests 
that Methanobrevibacter and Methanomassiliicoccus play essential roles in 
the methanogenesis of AD. From the PCA plots of the archaea (see 
Supplementary Material), it can be seen that there are some differences 
in the archaeal community in both the hydrolysis stage and the meth­
anogenic stage; this may be due to the different effects of different NBW 
on the microbial activity (Wang et al., 2023). 
Compared with Day 8, a decrease in the relative abundance (RA) of 
Bacteroidetes was observed on Day 35. Based on the RA results compared 
on Day 8, N2 (35.0 %) > control (32.4 %) > He (29.2 %) > CO2 (28.7 %) 
> Air (23.7 %) (Fig. 3b). While the RA of Bacteroidetes was the least in 
Air, probably because Air-NBW was the best for AD and hydrolysis, so 
the hydrolysis stage ended the earliest in Air. This conclusion is in line 
with other findings in the literature that Bacteroidetes are protein- 
degrading bacteria (Meng et al., 2023). The RA of Proteobacteria 
decreased from 25.1-29.8 % to 19.3–24.2 % mainly due to the hydrolysis 
rate change. Proteobacteria encompasses bacteria that participate in the 
preliminary breakdown of biomass, chiefly producing propionate, 
butyrate, and acetate, which follow the findings presented in this paper 
(Ariesyady et al., 2007). Following comparative analysis, the RA of 
Firmicutes rose (from 5.5-5.8 % to 10.1–21.5 %). Firmicutes are anabolic 
nutrient bacteria acting on VFA to produce H2 to be utilized by hydro­
genotrophic methanogens, which is in line with the phenomenon (Park 
et al., 2023). Bacteoidetes, Firmicutes, and Proteobacteria can all be 
involved in the hydrolysis of lignocellulose (Meng et al., 2023). After 
correlation analysis of bacteria with anaerobic environmental factors, a 
notable positive correlation was observed (p < 0.05) between Proteo­
bacteria and cumulative methane production (Fig. 3d); probably because 
Proteobacteria actively participated in the hydrolysis of AD (Ariesyady 
et al., 2007). The PCA of the bacteria showed some differences in the 
bacterial community during the hydrolysis stage, but the differences 
were not significant (see Supplementary Material); probably because 
this study was a mesophilic AD and the bacterial community changed 
more slowly (Siqueira et al., 2022). The bacterial community in the

3.3. Dewaterability 
The particle size distribution of digestate is intimately connected to 
its dewaterability (Zhang et al., 2024). The digesters with added NBW 
(Air, CO2, He, and N2) decreased digestate size (d50) by 30.8 %, 29.7 %, 
31.2 %, and 23.0 % compared with the control (Fig. 4a). The addition of

NBW enhances sludge degradation, which leads to a reduction in 
digestate particle size (He et al., 2022). It has been reported that the 
more thoroughly AD is carried out, the smaller the digestate particle size 
(Liang et al., 2022). When the digestate particle size exceeds 100 μm, the 
reduced dimensions of digestate particles contribute to enhanced dew­
aterability (Ward et al., 2023). Oversized digestate particles may have 
more water encapsulated inside, which is weakly bound to the particles 
and can be easily released during the dewatering process (Lin et al., 
2019). 
Zeta potential is a critical indicator for assessing the charge repel­
lency of the digestate interface (Cao et al., 2023). At the end of AD, the 
zeta potential of control became −13.7 ± 1.6 mV, and that of Air, CO2, 
He, and N2 became −12.8 ± 1.1 mV, −13.8 ± 1.1 mV, −11.8 ± 0.8 mV, 
and −13.4 ± 2.5 mV (Fig. 4a). The addition of NBW increased the zeta 
potential of digestate, probably due to the high surface activity of the 
bubbles in the NBW, this modification affected the electrostatic distri­
bution across the particle interfaces, resulting in elevated zeta potential 
(Kurz et al., 2021); while the addition of CO2-NBW slightly increased the 
zeta potential of DS, probably because the tiny bubbles in the CO2-NBW 
increased the collision frequency between the digestate particles, which 
led to a decrease in the zeta potential of DWS (He et al., 2022). The 
digestate zeta potential decreased from −20.6 mV to −29.4 mV due to 
pretreatment, leading to the deterioration of digestate dewaterability, a 
pattern similar to that of the present study (Cao et al., 2023). 
There is a strong correlation between the hydrophobicity of digestate 
and protein secondary structure (Liang et al., 2022). The addition of 
NBW led to a general rise in the proportion of β-sheet and β-turn 
structures, with a marked reduction in the proportion of α-helix and 
random coil conformations (see Supplementary Material). In addition, 
the α-helix/(β-sheet + random) ratio is often used to characterize the 
compositional features of protein secondary structure (Zhang et al., 
2024). A decrease in this ratio indicates a looser structure of the protein 
molecule (Estevam et al., 2024). The α-helix/(β-sheet + random) ratio of 
digestate in control was 0.46, while the ratios of the experimental group 
with the addition of NBW were 0.39, 0.39, 0.33, and 0.32, respectively 
(see Supplementary Material). The EPS structure of digestate gradually 
changed from “tightly ordered” to “loosely disordered”, and the loose 
structure of the protein in EPS exposed more internal hydrophobic 
groups (Hou et al., 2015). 
EPS is a class of polymers secreted by microbial cells that are tightly 
bound to the cells (Zhang et al., 2024). EPS in digestate can be catego­
rized into soluble EPS (S-EPS), loose layer EPS (LB-EPS), and tightly 
bound EPS (TB-EPS) (Hou et al., 2015). The trend of EPS within all di­
gesters remained consistent, with a gradual decrease in EPS with AD (see 
Supplementary Material). As the AD progressed, the protein content in 
the S-EPS decreased by 61.1–65.8 % compared with that before AD, 
while the polysaccharide content increased and then decreased. The EPS 
in this study showed a decreasing trend, which could be attributed to the 
consumption of proteins and polysaccharides in the sludge by AD 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021). 
The 3D-EEM plots of EPS extracted from digestate were investigated; 
the higher the fluorescence intensity of S-EPS, the worse the digestate 
dewaterability, and the higher the fluorescence intensity of TB-EPS, the 
better the digestate dewaterability (Simoni et al., 2024). Compared with 
the control, there was a reduction in complexine, tryptophan, fulvic 
acid, and soluble microbial byproducts in the digesters with the addition 
of NBW in the S-EPS (see Supplementary Material). The fluorescence 
region of control for TB-EPS was smaller than that of Air, CO2, He, and 
N2. In terms of the comparison of peak heights of humic acid, Air 
(329.3) > CO2 (220.2) > He (158.0) > N2 (154.9) > control (151.9). 
When more biopolymers from TB-EPS were extracted into S-EPS, the 
dewaterability was poorer (Chuenchart et al., 2021). 
CST is an indicator for assessing digestate dewaterability (Zhang 
et al., 2024). On Day 35, the digesters with added NBW (Air, CO2, He, 
and N2) decreased CST by 18.3 % (p < 0.01), 16.5 % (p < 0.01), 15.1 % 
(p < 0.01), and 15.1 % (p < 0.01) compared with the control (Fig. 5a); 
indicating that the addition of NBW had a good improvement on the 
dewaterability of digestate. This may be due to NBW destroying the 
hydrophobic layer on the surface of digestate particles, thus favoring 
digestate dewaterability (Patel et al., 2021). Four proteins in S-EPS 
exhibited a favorable association with CST (p < 0.05), indicating that the 
dewaterability gradually deteriorated with increased protein content in 
S-EPS. Proteins are very attractive to water, and as the percentage of 
proteins in the EPS increases, the worse the dewaterability of the EPS 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021). The α-helix also demonstrated a constructive 
correlation with CST (p < 0.001), whereas β-sheet (p < 0.05) showed a 
negative correlation (Fig. 5e). The decrease in the ratio of α-helix/ 
(β-sheet + random) indicates that the PN molecular structure is looser 
and enhances the hydrophobicity of digestate (Liang et al., 2022). Also, 
Air-NBW has the highest ratio in α-helix/(β-sheet + random), which 
indicates the best dewaterability of the digester with Air-NBW. The best 
improvement effect on DWS of AD with the addition of Air-NBW may be 
because Air-NBW can promote the degradation of organic matter and 
improve dewaterability (Fan et al., 2021b). 
SRF serves as a critical measure for assessing the filterability of 
digestate (Ward et al., 2023). When the SRF of digestate is greater than 
5 × 1012 m kg−1, the digestate has low dewaterability (Zhang et al., 
2024). The SRF of the initial sludge was (6.5 ± 1.0) × 1012 m kg−1, and 
after AD, the SRF of control increased to (20.6 ± 0.5) × 1012 m kg−1, and 
the dewaterability of digestate deteriorated. On Day 35, the digesters 
with added NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) decreased SRF by 29.5 % (p <
0.05), 33.0 % (p < 0.05), 32.8 % (p < 0.05), and 25.1 % (p < 0.05) 
compared with the control (Fig. 5c). Digestate particle size corroborates 
each other: the smaller the digestate particle size, the better the dew­
aterability (Fig. 4a). As the digestate particles become smaller, their 
specific surface area increases, this facilitates the expulsion of water and 
the separation from the digestate particles (Ward et al., 2023). SRF 
exhibited a marked positive correlation with two proteins in S-EPS (p <
0.05), α-helix (p < 0.001), β-sheet (p < 0.05), and random (p < 0.05) 
(Fig. 5e). It may be because the micro-nanobubbles in the NBW can take 
the digestate particles up in the process of rising to form the suspension 
state, which helps to the dispersion of the digestate particles and reduces 
their SRF (He et al., 2022). 
MC represents the proportion of the weight of water within the 
digestate relative to the aggregate weight of the digestate (Zhang et al., 
2024). On Day 35, the digesters with added NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) 
decreased MC by 19.5 % (p < 0.05), 16.7 % (p < 0.05), 14.6 % (p <
0.05), and 13.6% (p < 0.05) compared with control (Fig. 5d). Three 
proteins in TB-EPS exhibited a substantial inverse relationship to MC (p 
< 0.05), dewaterability was significantly reduced with the decrease of 
proteins in TB-EPS (Fig. 5e). Proteins in TB-EPS are involved in many 
biofilm functions, and a decrease in proteins may reduce the function­
ality of biofilms, thereby affecting water transport and dewaterability 
processes (Chuenchart et al., 2021). NBW presented a significant 
decrease in the MC of digestate, which might be related to the acceler­
ated decomposition of complex organic matter and small molecules by 
the addition of NBW (Zinjenab et al., 2023). 
Utilizing the collaborative validation from CST, SRF, and MC, it is 
determined that the dewaterability of digestate is compromised. In the 
dewaterability test after AD with NBW, CST, SRF, and MC were 
decreased by 15.1–18.3 %, 25.1–33.0 %, and 13.6–9.5 %, respectively. 
The addition of NBW reduced the digestate particle size by 23.0–30.8 %, 
and when the digestate particle size exceeded 100 μm. The reduction of 
digestate particle size helped to improve the dewaterability of the 
digestate (Ward et al., 2023). The introduction of NBW leads to an in­
crease in zeta potential in the AD system, which usually means an in­
crease in repulsive forces between digestate particles (Marcelino et al., 
2023). This may result in the digestate flocs becoming more loosely 
packed, thus improving the dewaterability of the digestate. The addition 
of NBW reduced the α-helix/(β-sheet + random) ratio by 15.2–30.4 %, 
which loosened the protein secondary structure, exposed more internal 
hydrophobic groups, and improved the dewaterability of the digestate

method to enhance the effectiveness of digestate compared with other

4. Conclusion 
A positive influence was observed in cumulative methane production 
from DWS and the dewaterability of digestate with the addition of NBW 
(Air, CO2, He, and N2), in which the most prominent effect was found in 
Air-NBW. The addition of Air-NBW increased protein decomposition and 
the cumulative methane production was improved by 27.8 %. Simul­
taneously, the indicators of dewaterability, i.e. CST, SRF, and MC were 
decreased by 18.2 %, 29.6 %, and 19.5 % respectively, after 35 days of 
digestion, as compared with the control. Overall, Air-NBW is the most 
cost-effective additive for AD of DWS.
